passage:
Note for Trisha's parents, Thursday
Trisha came in quiet today and didn't want her snack. When I asked, she said the class play list went up and her name wasn't on it. Then she said, very flatly, 'Mrs Pillai thinks I'm useless. She doesn't like me.' I asked how she knew. 'I just know. She looked at me when she read the names.' She said it three times, like something already checked. I didn't argue. I asked what else Mrs Pillai had said to her this week, and she remembered a 'good work' on her map. She went quiet at that. I suggested she ask Mrs Pillai about backstage jobs tomorrow, and she is thinking about it. You may want to talk it through tonight.
Deepika, after-school centre

qa.q: What did Trisha remember Mrs Pillai writing this week?
qa.a: Trisha remembered a 'good work' on her map.

qa.q: Why does 'Mrs Pillai thinks I'm useless' feel like a fact to Trisha?
qa.a: Trisha is hurt at being left off the list, and one look while the names were read seems to explain it; the hurt makes a guess feel as certain as something she was told.

qa.q: Which of Deepika's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Deepika didn't argue but asked what else Mrs Pillai had said, which let Trisha find a real piece of evidence, the 'good work', that didn't fit the belief.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pillai feel if she learned what Trisha believed?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai would likely be surprised and sorry, since she had praised Trisha's map that same week and may have had many reasons for the play list.

grounding: Shows a child left off a play list stating as fact that her teacher thinks she is useless, based only on a look.

passage:
Tuesday
Dear Diary,
Sir put up the list for the Annual Day play and I am NOT on it. Noor is the queen. Even Bilal got the lion and he can't remember lines. So now it is clear. Sir thinks I'm useless. He never smiles at me. Yesterday he said 'sit properly, Hafsa' and he didn't say it to anyone else. That proves it. Noor said maybe there are only eight parts and Sir chose the tall ones for the costumes, but Noor doesn't understand. I KNOW what he thinks. I am not putting my hand up in his class ever again. I didn't even eat Ammi's kheer tonight.
Hafsa

qa.q: Which part did Noor get in the play?
qa.a: Noor is the queen.

qa.q: Why does 'sit properly, Hafsa' feel like proof to Hafsa?
qa.a: Hafsa is hurt about the list and is hunting for a reason 😔, so an ordinary reminder looks like a sign of dislike, and the belief feels true without any real evidence.

qa.q: What could help Hafsa before deciding never to raise a hand again?
qa.a: Hafsa could ask Sir how the parts were chosen, or check Noor's idea about eight parts and costumes, before treating a guess as fact.

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Hafsa waves away the idea about eight parts?
qa.a: Noor might feel unheard and a little stuck, trying to help a friend who has already decided what Sir thinks.

grounding: Shows a child who was not cast in the play declaring in a diary, without evidence, that the teacher thinks they are useless.

passage: In the small school by the paddy fields outside Thodupuzha, Elizabeth Teacher chalked the names for the Children's Day skit on the board. Salma read them twice. Her name wasn't there. On the walk home along the canal, she kicked every stone she passed. 'Teacher hates me,' she told Umma at the gate. 'She thinks I'm useless.' 'Did she say so?' 'She doesn't have to. She gave the mango-seller part to Beena, and Beena can't even act.' Umma handed her a glass of water. 'And who reads the prayer every Monday?' Salma looked into the glass. 'Me.' 'Who chose you for that?' Salma didn't answer, but she stopped kicking the gatepost.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth Teacher writing the names for?
qa.a: The names were for the Children's Day skit.

qa.q: What does Salma kicking every stone suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: Salma is hurt and angry at being left out, and she has already turned it into a story that Elizabeth Teacher thinks she is useless, which feels certain to her.

qa.q: What turning point does Umma's question create?
qa.a: Asking who chose Salma to read the prayer puts one real fact against the guess, and Salma's silence shows the belief starting to loosen.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth Teacher see the skit list differently from Salma?
qa.a: Elizabeth Teacher may have chosen parts for many reasons, like giving Beena a turn, and may never have thought of it as a judgement on Salma at all.

grounding: Shows a village schoolgirl left out of a skit announcing as fact that her teacher thinks she is useless, with no evidence.

passage:
The cast list for the spring play was taped to the classroom door in Nairobi. Gabriel, nine, read it three times. Twenty-two names. Not his.

At home, he dropped his bag by the sofa. His sister Amara looked up from her maths.

"Ms Wanjiru thinks I'm useless," Gabriel said. "That's why."

"Did she say that?"

"She doesn't need to. When she read the list out she didn't even look at me. She looked at the window. And last week she made me redo my handwriting."

"She makes everyone redo handwriting."

"Not like me. She hates me. It's a fact."

Gabriel went to his room and lay facing the wall, sure of what Ms Wanjiru was thinking. It didn't occur to him that there were only twenty-two parts and twenty-eight children in the class.

qa.q: How many names were on the cast list?
qa.a: Twenty-two names.

qa.q: Why does Gabriel feel sure Ms Wanjiru hates him?
qa.a: Being left out hurt, and he fits small things, like her looking at the window and the handwriting, into that story. To him the hurt feels like proof, so he calls it a fact.

qa.q: What could help Gabriel test his belief instead of treating it as fact?
qa.a: He could ask Ms Wanjiru how parts were chosen, or count how many children missed out. Checking the real reasons is better than guessing what she thinks.

qa.q: How might Amara see Gabriel's certainty?
qa.a: Amara seems unconvinced, pointing out that everyone redoes handwriting. Amara might feel sorry for her brother but also frustrated that he won't listen.

grounding: A boy not chosen for the play decides his teacher thinks he is useless and states it as fact, with only thin evidence.

passage:
At the community centre drama club, Brother Thomas read out the roles for the Christmas play. Shepherds, angels, the innkeeper. Jomon, ten, waited for his name. It never came. He was put on "props and curtains".

Afterwards, while the others practised lines, he wound the curtain rope very tight.

"You okay?" asked Avni, who was also on props.

"Brother Thomas thinks I'm useless," Jomon said. "He knows I can't act. That's why he put me on curtains."

"You didn't even audition. You were at your cousin's wedding."

"He'd have given me nothing anyway. I know what he thinks."

"How?"

Jomon didn't answer. He just pulled the rope tighter. Across the hall, Brother Thomas was looking over at the props table, but Jomon kept his eyes on the floor.

qa.q: Why had Jomon missed the audition?
qa.a: Jomon was at his cousin's wedding.

qa.q: Why does "I know what he thinks" feel true to Jomon, even without evidence?
qa.a: Being left out stung, and blaming Brother Thomas's opinion gives the hurt a clear reason. Jomon trusts the feeling more than the fact that he missed the audition.

qa.q: What could Jomon try instead of guessing, and when would be a good moment?
qa.a: After practice he could ask Brother Thomas whether he can audition next time. Asking would replace a guess with a real answer.

qa.q: How might Avni see Jomon's belief?
qa.a: Avni seems to think it's unfair to Brother Thomas, because Jomon wasn't there for auditions. Avni may also be puzzled that Jomon won't explain how he knows.

grounding: A boy put on props for the play is certain the leader thinks he is useless, stating it as fact while ignoring that he missed auditions.

passage: In the government school at Palampur, the list for the Republic Day skit was pinned beside the water tank. Vidya read it twice. Her name wasn't there. On the walk home past the tea gardens she kicked every stone. 'Madam thinks I'm useless,' she told Tenzin. 'She thinks I can't even say two lines.' Tenzin shifted her schoolbag. 'Did she say that?' 'She doesn't need to. She never looks at me in class. She gave the queen's part to Kiran because Kiran is clever and I'm not.' 'Madam asked you to paint the backdrop last year,' Tenzin said. Vidya walked faster. 'That's different. That's just painting.'

qa.q: Where was the skit list pinned?
qa.a: It was pinned beside the water tank.

qa.q: Why did Vidya feel so sure Madam thought she was useless?
qa.a: She was hurt and disappointed at being left off the list, and that sting made her guess about Madam's thoughts feel like something she simply knew.

qa.q: What could Vidya do to check her belief?
qa.a: She could ask Madam how the parts were chosen, or remember facts like being asked to paint the backdrop, before deciding what Madam thinks.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Vidya's certainty?
qa.a: Tenzin doubts it, asking whether Madam actually said so and pointing to the backdrop, because she sees no real evidence.

grounding: A child not chosen for a skit states as fact that the teacher thinks she is useless, with no evidence.

passage: The class play parts went up on the board in Oslo on Tuesday afternoon, just before the bell. Wei got the troll. Ingrid got nothing: her name was under 'stage crew', with four others. On the tram home, she pressed her mitten against the fogged window. 'Mrs Halvorsen thinks I'm no good at anything,' she told her father. 'She thinks I'm boring and I'd ruin it.' Her father looked up from his phone. 'She said that?' 'She didn't have to. I could tell by her face when she read the list.' 'What was her face doing?' Ingrid frowned. She tried to remember, and couldn't. 'It was just... a face,' she said at last, more quietly.

qa.q: Which part did Wei get?
qa.a: Wei got the troll.

qa.q: What was Ingrid feeling on the tram, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was hurt and let down, pressing her mitten to the window, and that hurt made her guess about Mrs Halvorsen's thoughts feel certain.

qa.q: Why was her father's question about the teacher's face useful?
qa.a: It asked for real evidence, and when Ingrid couldn't remember any, she began to see her belief was a guess.

qa.q: How might Mrs Halvorsen explain the stage crew list?
qa.a: She might have reasons nobody on the tram knows, like needing reliable helpers backstage, which is why a guess about her thoughts can easily be wrong.

grounding: A child left off the cast list states as fact that the teacher thinks she is no good, based only on an imagined look.

passage: After evening study in the girls' hostel, Reena sat on her bunk with her knees pulled up. The annual day list had come out that afternoon, and Sangeeta Ma'am had not picked her for the dance drama. 'Sangeeta Ma'am thinks I'm useless,' she announced. 'She always has. She only picks the city girls.' Her bunkmate looked up from a geography map. 'She picked Lalitha, and Lalitha is from Karur.' 'That's one,' said Reena. 'Anyway, I saw how she looked at me in rehearsal. Like I was wasting her time.' She pulled the blanket over her head. When the warden came round for lights out, she stopped at Reena's bunk. 'Everything all right, kanna?' Reena said nothing, but she didn't pull her foot away when the warden patted it.

qa.q: Who did the bunkmate say was picked even though she is from Karur?
qa.a: The bunkmate said Lalitha was picked, and Lalitha is from Karur.

qa.q: Why did Reena state Sangeeta Ma'am's thoughts as if they were facts?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed at not being picked, so one look in rehearsal felt like proof and she didn't stop to check it.

qa.q: How could the warden help Reena test her belief?
qa.a: The warden could listen, then ask what Sangeeta Ma'am actually said and encourage Reena to ask how the dancers were chosen.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta Ma'am feel if she knew what Reena believed?
qa.a: She might be surprised and sorry, since a look in rehearsal can mean tiredness or concentration rather than a judgement about Reena.

grounding: A child not chosen for the dance drama declares that the teacher thinks she is useless, treating a look as proof.

passage:
Before, Monday: Shalini had practised the Queen's lines in the mirror all weekend. "I will be the Queen," she told her little brother.

During, Wednesday: Kavitha ma'am read out the cast. Queen: Rhea. Shalini: tree number two. Shalini's face burned. At lunch she told her friends, "Kavitha ma'am thinks I'm useless. She's always hated me." "Did she say that?" asked Rhea. "She doesn't have to," Shalini said. "I just know."

After, Friday: Kavitha ma'am kept Shalini back after class. "I made you a tree because I need you for the song at the end. You have the strongest voice in the class." Shalini stared. She had been so sure. She hadn't even asked.

qa.q: Which part did Shalini get in the play?
qa.a: Shalini got tree number two.

qa.q: Why did Shalini feel she "just knew" what Kavitha ma'am thought?
qa.a: Shalini felt hurt and disappointed, and her feeling seemed like proof, so she stated the teacher's dislike as fact.

qa.q: What could Shalini do next time she feels sure what someone thinks?
qa.a: Shalini could ask, for example "Why am I a tree?", instead of deciding the answer herself.

qa.q: What was Kavitha ma'am actually thinking when she cast Shalini as a tree?
qa.a: Kavitha ma'am was planning to use Shalini's strong voice for the song at the end, not thinking she was useless.

grounding: Over a week a girl not chosen as the Queen decides the teacher thinks she is useless, stating it as fact without evidence.

passage:
Akash, you think your teacher hates you because you're not in the play? Listen to your Gargi Dadi. When I was ten, in Allahabad, Sister Agnes chose girls for the Christmas play. I wasn't chosen at all. Not even as a shepherd.

I went home and cried. "Sister Agnes thinks I'm stupid. She never liked me. She looks at me like I'm a nuisance." I believed every word as if she had said it.

My mother asked, "Did she say that?" I said, "No, but I know."

The next week Sister Agnes called me to her room. She wanted me to read the story aloud from the side of the stage, because I read the most clearly in the class. The narrator! The most words of anyone.

I had spent a whole week sure of her thoughts. I was wrong about every single one.

qa.q: Who chose the girls for the Christmas play?
qa.a: Sister Agnes chose them.

qa.q: Why did young Gargi believe Sister Agnes thought she was stupid?
qa.a: Young Gargi felt rejected and hurt at not being chosen, and treated her own guesses about the teacher as if they had been said aloud.

qa.q: What question in the story could have saved Gargi a week of pain?
qa.a: Her mother's "Did she say that?" pointed to checking; asking Sister Agnes directly would have revealed the narrator role sooner.

qa.q: What was Sister Agnes actually thinking about Gargi?
qa.a: Sister Agnes thought Gargi read the most clearly in the class and wanted her as the narrator.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being sure, as a girl left out of a play, that her teacher thought her stupid, and being wrong.

passage:
It was the week the family was shifting flats, everything in cardboard boxes, and Disha had no time to practise. On Tuesday Sangeeta ma'am put up the list for the annual day dance. Disha's name wasn't on it.

She read it twice, then walked out stiffly. On the bus home she decided: Sangeeta ma'am thinks I'm clumsy. She saw me trip in PT. She thinks I'll ruin the dance. She probably laughs about me in the staff room.

At home she sat on a box and wouldn't unpack. "Ma'am hates me," she told her father, who was taping up kitchen boxes.
"Did she say so?"
"No. But it's obvious."
"Is it? Or is it just the story you're telling?"
Disha scowled. The next day, still grumpy, she asked Sangeeta ma'am. "You were absent for the auditions, Disha," ma'am said. "The shift, remember? There's a second group next week."

qa.q: Why was Disha's name not on the list?
qa.a: Disha was absent for the auditions because of the shift.

qa.q: Why did Disha feel so sure Sangeeta ma'am thought she was clumsy?
qa.a: Disha felt hurt and embarrassed, and in a stressful week her worry about tripping in PT turned into "facts" about her teacher's thoughts.

qa.q: Which choice turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Asking Sangeeta ma'am directly, even while grumpy, replaced the imagined story with the real reason and a second chance.

qa.q: How might Disha's father see the situation while taping boxes?
qa.a: Disha's father seems calm and gently doubtful, asking whether it is fact or just the story she is telling.

grounding: During a house move a girl left off the dance list decides her teacher thinks she is clumsy, until she asks.

passage: The Diwali assembly list went up on the notice board of the Andheri school. Preeti read it three times. Her name wasn't there. Not as Sita, not as a dancer, not even in the chorus. At home she threw her bag down. "Gautam sir hates me. He thinks I'm useless." Her mother looked up from the rangoli colours. "Did he say that?" "He doesn't have to say it. I know." "What did he say at the auditions?" Preeti thought. "He said my voice was clear." "Anything else?" "He said try again for the annual day." Preeti sat on the floor and began mixing yellow into orange. "He still hates me," she muttered. But she said it much more quietly this time.

qa.q: What did Gautam sir say about Preeti's voice at the auditions?
qa.a: He said her voice was clear.

qa.q: Why is Preeti so sure Gautam sir hates her?
qa.a: Preeti feels hurt and rejected at not being chosen, and treats that feeling as proof of what the teacher thinks, without any evidence.

qa.q: What could Preeti do to check the story in her head?
qa.a: She could ask Gautam sir what to work on for the annual day, and hear his real answer instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Gautam sir see Preeti, going by what he said at the auditions?
qa.a: He seems to think well of her voice and wants her to try again, not that she is useless.

grounding: A girl left out of the Diwali assembly declares her teacher thinks she is useless, stating the belief as fact with no evidence.

passage:
"Ritu, why aren't you eating the sheer khurma?"
"Not hungry."
Tanvir sat next to her on the Eid rug. "Is this about the Independence Day skit?"
"Rizwana ma'am didn't pick me. She picked everyone else."
"Not everyone. I didn't get picked either."
"But she hates me. She thinks I'm the worst in the class."
"Did she say that?"
"No. But she looked at me funny."
"Funny how?"
"Like... I don't know. Like she thought I was useless."
"Maybe she was thinking about lunch."
Ritu almost smiled. "It's not funny."
"Okay. But you're saying what she thinks, and she never said it."
"I just know."
"Last week she put your drawing on the board."
Ritu stopped. "That was different."
"Was it?"
Ritu took a spoon of sheer khurma. She didn't answer.

qa.q: Where did the teacher put Ritu's drawing last week?
qa.a: She put Ritu's drawing on the board.

qa.q: Why does Ritu believe Rizwana ma'am thinks she is useless?
qa.a: Ritu feels hurt and left out after the skit, and reads a look as proof, even though the teacher never said it.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do well in this talk?
qa.a: He gently asked for evidence and reminded Ritu about the drawing, without mocking her feelings.

qa.q: How might Rizwana ma'am see Ritu, going by the drawing on the board?
qa.a: She seems to value Ritu's work, so she might be surprised to learn Ritu thinks she is disliked.

grounding: During Eid a girl not chosen for a school skit insists the teacher thinks she is useless, stating it as fact while a friend asks for evidence.

passage:
When I was in Class 5, our school did an Onam pageant, and Chetan sir chose who would be Mahabali. I wanted it so badly. I practised the walk at home with a bedsheet cape. He chose Anoop.
I decided right away: Chetan sir thinks I'm useless. I even told Amma, "He doesn't like me, that's why." I didn't have one reason. It just felt true, so I said it like a fact.
I sulked the whole festival. At the pageant I didn't even clap.
Two weeks later, Chetan sir asked me to read the welcome speech for the district inspector. I was so confused. Later I found out Anoop was chosen because he was the tallest and the costume only fit him.
I still remember how sure I was, with zero proof.
— Kishore

qa.q: Why was Anoop chosen to be Mahabali?
qa.a: Anoop was chosen because he was the tallest and the costume only fit him.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after not being chosen, and why did the belief seem true?
qa.a: Kishore felt hurt and jealous, and that strong feeling made the idea that the teacher thought Kishore was useless feel like a fact.

qa.q: What could Kishore have done instead of deciding what Chetan sir thought?
qa.a: Kishore could have asked Chetan sir why Anoop was chosen, and would have heard about the costume.

qa.q: What would change if Kishore had known about the costume from the start?
qa.a: Kishore might still have felt disappointed, but would not have sulked through Onam believing the teacher disliked them.

grounding: A child looks back on being sure, with no evidence, that a teacher thought them useless after not being chosen for an Onam pageant.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Christmas play week.
Today Vinita stopped coming to rehearsal to watch. When I asked why, she said, very certainly, "You think I'm useless. That's why you didn't give me a part." She said it like a fact she had read somewhere.
In truth I had picked names from a bowl, because twenty-two children wanted eleven roles, and I had planned to ask her to narrate next term's play because she reads beautifully. Anand, who also wasn't picked, told her it was a lottery, but she shook her head.
Next step: I showed her the bowl with the leftover name slips and asked if she would help with the stage lights this week. She agreed, but she is still watching my face very carefully.

qa.q: How did the teacher choose who got parts?
qa.a: By picking names from a bowl, because twenty-two children wanted eleven roles.

qa.q: Why did Vinita say the teacher thinks she is useless?
qa.a: She felt hurt and rejected at not getting a part, and her guess about the teacher's thoughts felt like certain fact without any evidence.

qa.q: What did the teacher do, and what else could help?
qa.a: Showing the bowl and offering the stage-lights job gave evidence against the belief; telling Vinita about the narrator plan could help further.

qa.q: How does Anand see not being picked?
qa.a: Anand sees it as a lottery, not a judgement, which is why he tries to tell Vinita so.

grounding: A child not chosen for the class play decides the teacher thinks she is useless and states it as fact.
